newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somali warlord urges Ethiopia to withdraw troops.
newsitem.headline: Somali warlord urges Ethiopia to withdraw troops.

text.p: Somali warlord Hussein Mohamed Aideed on Thursday urged Ethiopia to immediately withdraw its forces which invaded parts of western Somalia last week.

Ethiopia, in its first comment on the border situation, said on Wednesday that its defence forces killed or wounded more than 100 Moslem fundamentalists who had tried to attack the border town of Dollo.

Aideed's statement, which accused Ethiopia of "unacceptable aggression", stopped short of expressing support for al-Ittihad, the Moslem fundamentalist group against which the Ethiopian attack was aimed.
It said Aideed's government was opposed to any group destabilising the area and urged Ethiopia to withdraw its forces "immediately and unconditionally".
Another Somali leader, Mohamed Ali Abdi, deputy chairman of the Somali National Front (SNF), said on Thursday the SNF had decided to join the fight against Ethiopian forces.
He said the Ethiopians had ignored peace initiatives from Kenyan officials at the Kenyan border town of Mandera.
Abdi said women and children had been evacuated from the town of Bulo Hawo for fear of an Ethiopian attack there.
A spokesman for al-Ittihad said the Ethiopians might resume their attacks after the New Year.
In Addis Ababa, the state-owned Amharic-language daily Addis Zemen urged support for the army against Moslem fundamentalists who it said had tried to attack Dollo from Somalia.

"The action taken by the defence forces to crush the terrorist group was praiseworthy. It shows to all those who may have similar designs to violate the country's sovereignty that they would be dealt with without mercy," it said on Thursday.

The ethiopian statement on Wednesday said those killed included Arabs from a number of countries. It gave no indication of Ethiopian casualties and did not say how far Ethiopian forces had penetrated into Somalia.

It was the second time in four months that Ethiopian forces had crossed into Somalia to attack al-Ittihad forces. Last August Ethiopia said its forces killed more than 230 fighters of the group and destroyed three of their camps in eastern Somalia.
Somalia has had no government since 1991 when the ouster of dictator Mohamed Siad Barre was followed by a bitter civil war.
